questions.q: Which explorer's 1492 voyage opened lasting contact between Europe and the Americas?
questions.explain: Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean in October 1492. His voyage began the Columbian Exchange of crops, animals and diseases.

questions.q: Which food crop, first grown in the Andes, spread to Europe after 1492 and helped its population grow?
questions.explain: The potato, carried to Europe through the Columbian Exchange, was cheap and calorie-rich. It became a staple from Ireland to Russia.

questions.q: Which 1507 map, now kept at the Library of Congress, was the first to print the name "America"?
questions.explain: Martin Waldseemuller's wall map named the New World after Amerigo Vespucci. The Library of Congress bought it from Germany in 2003.

questions.q: Which English settlement, founded in 1607, was the first permanent one in North America?
questions.explain: Jamestown, Virginia, survived early starvation by growing tobacco for export. It became the base of the Virginia colony.

questions.q: In 1619, the first documented enslaved Africans in English North America arrived in which colony?
questions.explain: A ship landed about twenty enslaved Africans at Point Comfort, Virginia, in 1619. Slavery then spread across the colonies.

questions.q: Which 1620 agreement, signed aboard a ship, set up self-government for the Plymouth colonists?
questions.explain: Settlers who landed outside Virginia's charter promised to obey laws made by the community. It is an early example of consent-based government.

questions.q: The 1735 libel trial of which New York printer helped establish that truth is a defense against charges of libel?
questions.explain: Zenger's jury acquitted him after his lawyer argued that printing the truth could not be libel. The case became a symbol of press freedom.

questions.q: Preachers such as Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield led which colonial religious revival of the 1730s and 1740s?
questions.explain: The Great Awakening stressed personal conversion and drew crowds across denominations. It also weakened some established churches' authority.

questions.q: Which 1776 document, mainly written by Thomas Jefferson, announced the colonies' break from Britain?
questions.explain: The Declaration listed grievances against King George III and argued that governments get their power from the consent of the governed.

questions.q: Colonists protested "taxation without representation" after Britain taxed printed materials in 1765 with which law?
questions.explain: The Stamp Act required a tax stamp on newspapers, legal papers and playing cards. Colonial protests led Parliament to repeal it in 1766.

questions.q: Which 1787 deal gave every state equal votes in the Senate and population-based seats in the House?
questions.explain: Delegates at the Constitutional Convention settled a fight between large and small states by creating a two-house Congress.

questions.q: Who served as the first Chief Justice of the United States?
questions.explain: George Washington appointed John Jay in 1789. John Marshall, who served much longer, was the fourth Chief Justice.

questions.q: Which first Treasury Secretary proposed a national bank and federal assumption of state war debts?
questions.explain: Hamilton's financial plan tied wealthy creditors to the new government. Jefferson and Madison opposed it, helping form the first party system.

questions.q: Which 1803 purchase from France roughly doubled the size of the United States?
questions.explain: Jefferson bought about 828,000 square miles for roughly $15 million. Lewis and Clark soon set out to explore it.

questions.q: Which 1803 Supreme Court case established the power of judicial review?
questions.explain: Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that the Court can strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution.

questions.q: Which president signed the Indian Removal Act of 1830?
questions.explain: The law let the government exchange Native lands in the Southeast for territory west of the Mississippi. It led to the Trail of Tears.

questions.q: In August 1814, British troops burned the Capitol and the President's House during which conflict?
questions.explain: Dolley Madison saved a portrait of Washington before the British set fire to the city. Both buildings were later rebuilt.

questions.q: Which 1848 meeting in New York issued the Declaration of Sentiments on women's rights?
questions.explain: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott led it. The Declaration of Sentiments called for women's right to vote.

questions.q: Which president issued the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863?
questions.explain: The proclamation declared enslaved people in Confederate-held areas free and let Black men join the Union army.

questions.q: What did the Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in 1865, do?
options: It guaranteed equal protection of the laws
questions.explain: The amendment banned slavery and involuntary servitude except as punishment for a crime. Congress passed it before the war ended.

questions.q: Which amendment, ratified in 1868, guaranteed citizenship and equal protection of the laws?
questions.explain: The Fourteenth Amendment overturned Dred Scott and became the base for most later civil rights cases.

questions.q: Which 1857 Supreme Court decision held that Black Americans could not be citizens?
questions.explain: Chief Justice Roger Taney wrote that people of African descent had no rights the government must respect. It helped push the nation toward war.

questions.q: Which Union general accepted Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox in April 1865?
questions.explain: Grant offered generous terms, letting Lee's men keep their horses and go home. Arlington stands on Lee's former estate.

questions.q: Which formerly enslaved abolitionist lived at Cedar Hill in Anacostia and served as U.S. Marshal for the District?
questions.explain: Douglass escaped slavery in 1838 and became a writer, speaker and adviser to Lincoln. He lived at Cedar Hill from 1878 until 1895.

questions.q: Which 1883 law created a merit-based civil service after a disappointed office-seeker shot President Garfield?
questions.explain: The Pendleton Act required that many federal jobs be filled by competitive exams rather than political favors.

questions.q: What was the main aim of the 1887 Dawes Act?
options: To divide tribal land into individual allotments
questions.explain: The Dawes Act pushed Native families toward private farming. Reservation land fell by about two thirds, and tribes lost millions of acres.

questions.q: Which 1896 Supreme Court case upheld "separate but equal" segregation?
questions.explain: The Court upheld a Louisiana railway law, giving legal cover to Jim Crow until Brown v. Board of Education in 1954.

questions.q: Which president led the nation through the Great Depression and most of World War II?
questions.explain: Roosevelt won four elections, from 1932 to 1944, and died in office in April 1945.

questions.q: Which New Deal agency put millions of unemployed Americans to work on public projects such as roads, schools and murals?
questions.explain: The WPA, created in 1935, employed about 8.5 million people over its eight-year life.

questions.q: Which amendment, ratified in 1920, guaranteed women the right to vote?
questions.explain: After decades of activism, the Nineteenth Amendment barred states from denying the vote on account of sex.

questions.q: Which event on December 7, 1941 brought the United States into World War II?
questions.explain: Japanese aircraft struck the Pacific fleet in Hawaii. Congress declared war on Japan the next day.

questions.q: Which 1944 Supreme Court decision upheld the wartime removal of Japanese Americans from the West Coast?
questions.explain: The Court accepted the claim of military necessity. Congress apologized and paid redress to survivors in 1988.

questions.q: Which 1954 Supreme Court case ruled that racial segregation in public schools is unconstitutional?
questions.explain: A unanimous Court, led by Chief Justice Earl Warren, held that separate schools are inherently unequal.

questions.q: At the 1963 March on Washington, Martin Luther King Jr. delivered which famous speech?
questions.explain: King spoke from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial to a crowd of about 250,000.

questions.q: Which 1964 law banned discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin?
questions.explain: After a long Senate filibuster, President Johnson signed the act in July 1964. It ended legal segregation in public places.

questions.q: The Vietnam Veterans Memorial was designed by which Yale undergraduate?
questions.explain: Maya Lin won an open design contest in 1981 with a black granite wall. Critics first called it too plain, but it is now beloved.

questions.q: Which 1962 standoff between the United States and the Soviet Union nearly led to nuclear war?
questions.explain: President Kennedy demanded the removal of Soviet missiles from Cuba. After 13 tense days, Moscow agreed.

questions.q: On September 11, 2001, hijacked planes struck the World Trade Center and which Virginia building?
questions.explain: The attack killed 184 people at the Pentagon. It led to the war in Afghanistan and the creation of the Department of Homeland Security.

questions.q: Who became the first African American president in 2009?
questions.explain: Obama won the 2008 election and served two terms. The museum on the Mall opened during his presidency, in 2016.

questions.q: Which 2015 Supreme Court decision required every state to recognize same-sex marriages?
questions.explain: By a 5-4 vote, the Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment protects the right to marry.
